# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–37 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 2)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of tenth year after Waterloo (1831). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapter 37 (spring). Emperor of China dinner scheduled Monday, 8th July; election for Westminster borough Tuesday, 9th July (three weeks ahead as of Chapter 35). Chapter 36 set in market towns and London. Chapter 37 set in Harrowgate (hill farms) and market towns (Bryngate, Salwick); references to Southend, Brighton, Penzance, Orkney, Lowestoft; interspersed vignettes of provincial life.
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; coastal towns (Lowestoft, Penzance, Brighton); rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, Staveton, Bryngate, Salwick, Beccles).

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident with Felix and Henrietta. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter by six o'clock evening, sent via Didon to Pall Mall East. Full of regrets; in debt. Chapter 36: Attended soirée with Roger Carbury; found Paul and Henrietta together upon return. Disbelieved accidental visit claim. Cross-examined Henrietta on intentions. Allowed Henrietta to leave after kissing. **Chapter 37: Expressed wonder at Alf (editor of "Evening Pulpit"), noting he has sailed "within the wind" (stayed within legal bounds) but now risks three or four thousand pounds in legal expenses by attempting to prove something (nature unspecified).**

**Felix Carbury**: Beautiful; cynosure of mother's eyes. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won £200 cheque from Melmotte if withdrew from Marie. **Chapter 37: Amenable to elopement with Marie planned for Thursday week (departure from Liverpool noon). Didon (Marie's attendant) "very urgent" he recover funds intrusted to Melmotte. Frequently at City Road Music-Hall evenings late. Mind "ever in Grosvenor Square." Avoids giving direct reply to Ruby's importunities. When Ruby pressed demand for marriage declaration, Felix refused outright: "Marry, Ruby! No, I don't ever mean to marry. It's the greatest bore out." Deemed such a lie beneath his baronetcy; considered young women didn't truly believe promises but liked being deceived later. Views journey to New York as escape from trouble; thinks lies to young women carry no weight. Has not told Ruby of departure plans. Suggested Ruby dance at City Road Music-Hall.**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew (Chapter 32 evening); determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 36: Paul visited her at Welbeck Street in Lady Carbury's absence. Felt caught when discovered together though innocent. Told mother: "He is so much above me, that, though I do love him, I cannot think of him in that way. And I have told you that I do love some one else." Praised Roger as "rock of strength" who "never lies."

## Ruby Ruggles
Granddaughter of Daniel Ruggles (Sheep's Acre). Pretty with long glossy ringlets. **Chapter 36: Now in London, working as servant/maid to Mrs. Pipkin (her aunt, mother's brother's widow) at Islington who lets lodgings with five children. Chapter 37: Reported to Felix that Paul Montague told Squire he'd seen her, and Squire coming about John Crumb. Ruby's grandfather says "whoever it is ought to speak out his mind" and "A girl has to mind herself, though she's ever so fond of a young man." Ruby "very fond of dancing—perhaps liked it better than anything in the world." Danced with Felix at City Road Music-Hall.**

**Chapter 37 Crisis—Squire Roger's Intervention**: **Felix refused Ruby's marriage demand. Ruby stopped him in the street, shocked he would court her without intending marriage. When Felix left her, Roger Carbury visited Ruby at Mrs. Pipkin's house. Ruby disclosed her grandfather Daniel Ruggles had pulled her by the hairs of her head, tearing her things, nearly getting into bed—behavior witnessed by Sally Hockett. She fled to protect herself. Roger, knowing Daniel's violent disposition under gin's influence, didn't fault her coming to her aunt, but warned: Felix "is as bad as bad can be...would ruin you and cast you from him without a pang of remorse. He has no heart." Roger praised John Crumb as noble, loving, wanting only her happiness and respectability, not disgrace. Declared: "He loves you after that fashion that he wants to make you happy and respectable...He thinks more of you than of himself." Ruby, "never expected to hear any one call John Crumb noble," found conviction borne upon her though she struggled against it—viewing Crumb's nobility as "dusty, mealy,--and also...dumb." Roger warned if Felix and John Crumb were alone together, something would happen to Felix. Roger spoke to Mrs. Pipkin about Ruby's late hours; promised money if she wished to go home; extracted promise she would not see Felix again. His words weakened her admiration for Felix though she had not fully embraced John Crumb.**

**John Crumb**: Country lover from Suffolk, "Bungay mealman." Chapter 35: After supper, moved to take Ruby's hand; Ruby fled. Rode to Carbury Hall searching for her. Chapter 36: Communicating with Ruby and searching for her. **Chapter 37: Daniel Ruggles describes him as "regular enough" if Ruby let him; "like clockwork—only the slowest clock out." Roger views him as noble, loving, gallant; capable of forgiving everything if Ruby returns, but will "see the matter out" if she does not, persisting in slow fashion of his own.**

**Daniel Ruggles**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm on bishop's lease; Roger Carbury's tenant. Chapter 36: Reconciled to loss of Ruby. **Chapter 37: Violent under gin and water; pulled Ruby by hair when she was undressed and getting into bed (witnessed by Sally Hockett). Told Roger "whoever it is ought to speak out his mind"; says "a girl has to mind herself."**

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Chairman, South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Big man with large whiskers; expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. Rumours of gigantic swindler. Candidate for Westminster parliament seat. Planning Emperor of China dinner (8th July, Monday) and Westminster election (9th July, Tuesday). Chapter 36: Called Paul to Grosvenor Square, emphasized unanimity essential; offered Paul £6,000 to accept and leave or go abroad; Paul agreed to consider. **Chapter 37: Paul promised to see Melmotte before next Board day. Proximity of dinner and election days distressing to some Melmottites, though accidental; much to be done about both.**

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well; forming own opinions. Rejected Lord Grasslough. **Chapter 36: Devised elopement plan with Felix: Travel to Liverpool, board S.S. "Adriatic" Thursday week at noon bound for New York. Marry on board or at New York. Return within month to force father's acceptance. Didon to pose as aunt; Felix as American "Smith"; Marie as French girl. Had key to Grosvenor Square gardens; arranged Didon to unlock gate. Chapter 37: Felix thinks perhaps emissary from Marie (perhaps Didon herself) had visited him.** Chapter 35: Engaged to Lord Nidderdale.

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no London expenses; family will not return from Caversham. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham from debt. Dolly refused consent unless half produce given to him.

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Made protest against Melmottes. Following morning received invitation to stay with them. By Sunday, present at Grosvenor Square.

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has rooms in Bruton Street. States father cannot sell Pickering without his consent.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco/Chicago line, through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium "to run them up even to 110." Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Situation**: Living at Beargarden. Junior railway firm member. Dislikes Fisker. Trembles for his money. Thoroughly in love with Hetta. Chapter 36: Returned from Liverpool Friday morning. Resolved to tell Mrs. Hurtle face-to-face he would not marry her. After Board Sunday morning, visited Melmotte. Walked with Roger to his hotel. Confided Mrs. Hurtle in London; been with her three or four times. Told Roger all—rumoured duel, rumoured murder, rumour of existing husband. Declared: "But even if the rumours be untrue I will not marry her." Roger urged him to cheat "Devil" if bargain made. Saturday morning visited Islington; found Mrs. Hurtle out for day. Wrote note in pencil. Sunday morning: Left Melmotte; planned to visit Mrs. Hurtle at 7 o'clock evening.

**Chapter 37 Evening Visit to Islington**: **Paul visited Mrs. Hurtle. She received him warmly, regretted absence, explained she'd been to Southend with Mrs. Pipkin and baby for health (Harrowgate air "muggy"). Praised American humility. Urged him to pursue Mexican railway project; offered to accompany as companion. Paul deflected but tacitly admitted if journey made, she might be traveller. Conversation advanced him farther from declaring resolution never to marry. Mrs. Hurtle, leaning forward, elbows on knees, asked: "Must the purpose be told to-night?" She felt weak and cowardly; expressed solitude during last weeks; Mrs. Pipkin and baby insufficient. Begged: "if it be cruel, or harsh, or painful...then drop your purpose for to-night." Eyes showed "only love" (love which might be disappointed, but still love).**

**Later in Chapter 37**: **Mrs. Hurtle suggested travel to "little place that would be pretty" for health. Paul suggested Brighton; she objected as too fashionable. Discussed Penzance (refused), Orkney (refused). Paul suggested Lowestoft; she agreed with delight. She requested Paul take her down to Lowestoft: "It is desolate for a woman to go into such a place all alone. I will not ask you to stay." Paul made no answer, face troubled, brow black; "endeavouring to think--but he was only aware of his danger." Mrs. Hurtle pressed: "I don't think you will let me ask in vain for such a favour as that." Paul suggested Saturday, the 29th; must attend next Board and promised to see Melmotte before Board day. Mrs. Hurtle agreed. Asked if she should meet him at railway station; he undertook to come fetch her. As he took leave, she stood close, put cheek up for kiss. Paul took her in arms and kissed her lips as well as cheeks. His departure resolved nothing; confession deferred.**

**Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle**: Formerly betrothed to Paul. Arrived Wednesday. During earlier engagement promised to follow him; renewed promises in New York. Theatre evening: Paul took her. Does not like Frenchmen; prefers Englishmen to Americans. Thinks he should marry her or world hear story of his perjury. Most fond of baby, like Mrs. Pipkin. Now unwell, weak and cowardly; eyes show only love. Wants travel to pretty place near Lowestoft for health.

## Lord Nidderdale
Intent on marrying Marie for fortune. Chapter 35: Marie engaged to Nidderdale.

## Mr. Broune
Editor, "Morning Breakfast Table." Nearer fifty than sixty; young of his age. Chapter 35: Proposed to Lady Carbury. When he read her rejection letter: stood at fireplace, left letter on table. Felt admiration greater than ever.

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Works as priest on day-labourer's wages. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew (Chapter 32 evening); determination unshaken. Chapter 36: Attended soirée with Lady Carbury. Found Paul and Henrietta together. Walked with Paul to his hotel; confirmed fears regarding Felix and Ruby well founded. **Chapter 37: Visited Ruby at Islington; warned her forcefully against Felix; praised John Crumb's nobility and love; extracted promise she would not see Felix again. Spoke to Mrs. Pipkin about Ruby's late hours.**

## Minor Characters
**Miles Grendall**: Secretary to Melmotte. Does not pay debts of honour. Chapter 37: Elder Grendall (Lord Alfred) found Westminster electioneering nearly overwhelming; declared willingness to help Melmotte but nearly in rebellion; "If this goes on much longer I shall cut it." Both Grendalls driven by dinner and election preparations.

**Didon**: Marie's attendant; facilitates elopement plan; to receive £50 before boarding ship. **Chapter 37: "Very urgent" with Felix to recover funds intrusted to Melmotte.**

**Father John Barham**: Priest, Beccles.

**Mrs. Pipkin**: Ruby's aunt at Islington; lets lodgings with five children. Most fond of baby. Chapter 37: Roger spoke to her about Ruby's late hours.

**Sally Hockett**: Witnessed Daniel Ruggles pulling Ruby by hair.

**Chapter 37 Provincial Vignettes**: Neena Brackwood (sorted letters by candlelight, bought ribbon, laughed, mended sleeve), Dalde Brackwood (shrugged, sorted letters, argued over oats price, promised to teach Salwick children letters), Pebin Wexwood (left Harrowgate for Bryngate), Breena (followed Pebin within month), Orric (counted coins twice, came up penny short, argued with carter over sack of oats). Atmospheric details: vespers bell, frost silvering hedges, dog barking, gulls quarreling, threatened rain (held off), chalked crooked sun on forge wall, baker's boy late, line at oven grew long, bees humming in lavender behind parsonage, road all ruts and puddles after thaw.
